<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

Case sf_bq028: Data Quality Discovery Through Exploration ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">D.1.3 </span>Direct SQL Generation Result &amp; Analysis</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsubsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A4.SS1.SSS3.Px1" title="In D.1.3. Direct SQL Generation Result &amp; Analysis ‣ D.1. Case sf_bq028: Data Quality Discovery Through Exploration ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Generated SQL strategy:</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A4.SS1.SSS3.Px2" title="In D.1.3. Direct SQL Generation Result &amp; Analysis ‣ D.1. Case sf_bq028: Data Quality Discovery Through Exploration ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Result</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsubsection"><a href="#A4.SS1.SSS4" title="In D.1. Case sf_bq028: Data Quality Discovery Through Exploration ‣ Appendix D Case Study ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">D.1.4 </span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> Result &amp; Analysis</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsubsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A4.SS1.SSS4.Px1" title="In D.1.4. APEX-SQL Result &amp; Analysis ‣ D.1. </ol></li>

</span></span></span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">Received  5 June 2009</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Text-to-SQL systems powered by Large Language Models have excelled on academic benchmarks but struggle in complex enterprise environments. The primary limitation lies in their reliance on static schema representations, which fails to resolve semantic ambiguity and scale effectively to large, complex databases. To address this, we propose <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span>, an Agentic Text-to-SQL Framework that shifts the paradigm from passive translation to agentic exploration. Our framework employs a hypothesis-verification loop to ground model reasoning in real data.
In the schema linking phase, we use logical planning to verbalize hypotheses, dual-pathway pruning to reduce the search space, and parallel data profiling to validate column roles against real data, followed by global synthesis to ensure topological connectivity.
For SQL generation, we introduce a deterministic mechanism to retrieve exploration directives, allowing the agent to effectively explore data distributions, refine hypotheses, and generate semantically accurate SQLs.
Experiments on BIRD (70.65% execution accuracy) and Spider 2.0-Snow (51.01% execution accuracy) demonstrate that <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> outperforms competitive baselines with reduced token consumption.
Further analysis reveals that agentic exploration acts as a performance multiplier, unlocking the latent reasoning potential of foundation models in enterprise settings. Ablation studies confirm the critical contributions of each component in ensuring robust and accurate data analysis.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Agentic Text-to-SQL, Schema Linking, SQL Generation
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.16720v1/intro.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/320;" width="476" height="320" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1. </span>A comparison of Text-to-SQL paradigms. (a) <span id="S0.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Static Schema Prompting</span> relies solely on the schema, causing hallucinations when metadata is ambiguous. (b) <span id="S0.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pre-processed Schema Augmentation</span> attempts to enrich context with preliminary data profiling, yet introduces irrelevant noise and token overhead. (c) <span id="S0.F1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> introduces <span id="S0.F1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agentic Exploration</span>, employing a hypothesis-verification loop to actively interrogate the database and ground logical reasoning.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Text-to-SQL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> aims to make data analysis accessible by translating natural language questions into executable SQL queries. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly improved execution accuracy on academic benchmarks like Spider 1.0 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2018</a>)</cite> and BIRD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>. However, this performance drops substantially in real-world enterprise environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lei et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A fundamental limitation of current approaches lies in their reliance on passive perception.
Standard methods depend on static schema definitions (Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>a), but enterprise databases often feature opaque column names, hiding true semantics within data values rather than metadata. Without access to the data, models are forced to guess.
To address this, existing works attempt to inject pre-processed data profiles (Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>b). However, this approach has limitations. On one hand, static summaries remain detached from specific question contexts, failing to provide the exact evidence needed. On the other hand, covering the vast scale of databases introduces noise and incurs heavy token overhead.
Consequently, these passive paradigms disconnect reasoning from reality, leading to queries that are syntactically correct but semantically flawed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To resolve this, we propose a paradigm shift from passive perception to agentic exploration (Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>c). Central to our approach is a Hypothesis-Verification loop where the agent formulates logical assumptions based on the user question and validates them by executing exploratory SQLs against actual data. This process transforms Text-to-SQL from a static translation task into an interactive reasoning task grounded in database reality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span>, a unified framework applying agentic exploration to both Schema Linking and SQL Generation.
First, given massive industrial databases, Schema Linking is crucial to isolate the relevant schema elements before processing.
We employ Logical Planning to verbalize question requirements into schema-agnostic hypotheses, and introduce Dual-Pathway Pruning to compress the search space, making the subsequent validation feasible within large databases. The agent then conducts Parallel Data profiling to validate these hypotheses against real data, followed by Global Synthesis to ensure topological connectivity across the verified elements.
For SQL Generation, we bridge the gap between abstract intent and data-level constraints through Deterministic Guidance Retrieval, which maps logical steps into exploration directives.
Equipped with this guidance, the agent performs agentic exploration by navigating a flexible action space to profile data distributions, consolidate findings, and synthesize candidate queries. The process concludes with a final confirmation step to verify semantic fidelity against the accumulated evidence, ensuring the generated SQL is syntactically and semantically correct.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Extensive experiments on BIRD and Spider 2.0 validate this paradigm shift. On <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BIRD-Dev</span>, <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> achieves an execution accuracy of 70.7%, surpassing competitive baselines such as OpenSearch-SQL (69.3%) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and RSL-SQL (67.2%) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
On the enterprise-grade <span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spider 2.0-Snow</span>, <span id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> attains 51.0% execution accuracy, outperforming existing agentic systems like DSR-SQL (35.3%) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Further analysis reveals that agentic exploration acts as a performance multiplier, yielding up to an 18.33% absolute gain for high-capacity models like DeepSeek-V3.2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Test-time compute scaling evaluations show that our framework effectively unlocks the latent reasoning potential of foundation models.
Moreover, ablation studies demonstrate that key components such as logical planning and exploration are crucial for improving schema linking performance; deterministic guidance in SQL generation enhances exploration effectiveness and efficiency, allowing the agent to resolve implementation uncertainties in fewer interaction rounds.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions can be summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agentic Exploration for Schema Linking.</span> We propose a schema linking approach utilizing logical planning to verbalize hypotheses, dual-pathway pruning to reduce the massive search space, and parallel data profiling followed by global synthesis to ground column selection in empirical evidence.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agentic Exploration for SQL Generation.</span> We introduce an agentic SQL generation process where deterministic retrieval provides exploration directives for the agent to verify hypotheses and consolidate data findings, autonomously resolving implementation ambiguities before query synthesis.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Empirical Validation &amp; Insights.</span> We demonstrate superior performance on BIRD and Spider 2.0 benchmarks, outperforming competitive baselines. Our analysis confirms that agentic exploration serves as a performance multiplier and is a highly effective mechanism for robust data analysis in enterprise environments.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Static Schema Prompting.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To empower LLMs for Text-to-SQL tasks, standard approaches typically linearize database schemas and supply them alongside queries as prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. While methods such as DIN-SQL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023</a>)</cite> and DAIL-SQL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2023</a>)</cite> optimize prompt structures to enhance reasoning capabilities, a fundamental challenge remains: LLMs are inherently “blindness” to underlying data distribution. Real-world databases often contain ambiguous column names, opaque abbreviations, or domain-specific codes that are semantically indecipherable without access to actual data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>. Consequently, standard prompting confines models to surface-level schema representations, often inducing hallucinations when correct SQL logic depends on concrete data content rather than metadata alone.
To mitigate the uncertainty arising from this “blindness”, several works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pourreza et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Talaei et al., 2024</a>)</cite> generate multiple candidate SQL queries and employ consensus or ranking-based strategies to select the most plausible output.
<span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">However, these passive perception approaches still compel models to infer implementation details from ambiguous schemas. This severance of user intent from data reality frequently results in syntactically valid yet semantically flawed queries, particularly when the correct logic hinges on concealed data distributions.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pre-processed Schema Augmentation.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To bridge the gap between abstract schema definitions and concrete data values, recent research has introduced pre-processing pipelines to enrich schema representations. Approaches such as AskData <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shkapenyuk et al., 2025</a>)</cite> leverage data profiling and query log analysis to statically augment schemas with value distributions and historical join paths prior to inference. Similarly, TA-SQL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> employs LLMs to generate detailed natural-language descriptions for each database field. While these methods provide richer context, they rely on “pre-computed” knowledge that is static and often misaligned with the specific reasoning trajectory of a novel query.
<span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Despite offering additional context, these static augmentation strategies incur substantial token overhead and introduce irrelevant noise. By decoupling context retrieval from the evolving reasoning demands of complex queries, they fail to provide the targeted, dynamic verification necessary for accurate problem-solving.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.16720v1/framework.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/262;" width="476" height="262" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2. </span>The proposed <span id="S2.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> framework. <span id="S2.F2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Schema Linking (Top):</span> To navigate massive databases, <span id="S2.F2.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> first verbalizes a logical plan, serving as a grounded reference for subsequent pruning and verification. It actively verifies the semantic roles of candidate tables through parallel profiling and summarizes key observations for each column. Finally, <span id="S2.F2.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> refines the schema subgraph by ensuring topological connectivity and recovering missing dependencies via global synthesis. <span id="S2.F2.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SQL Generation (Bottom):</span> <span id="S2.F2.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> employs a deterministic retrieval mechanism to map logical operations to specific exploration guidance. Directed by these constraints, it navigates a flexible action space to autonomously profile data distributions, consolidate exploration findings, synthesize candidate queries, or perform a final confirmation check to validate the executable SQL.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agentic Exploration.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Contemporaneous literature have begun to adopt agentic workflows for database interaction. For instance, DSR-SQL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> utilizes a dual-state mechanism to manage context updates, while AutoLink <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> focuses on iterative schema exploration to resolve linking issues in massive databases. Furthermore, ReFoRCE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., [n. d.]</a>)</cite> introduces a column exploration mechanism to verify data values before generation. Although these methods mark a paradigm shift towards active problem-solving, they often treat schema linking and value verification as isolated sub-tasks or rely on unguided exploration, leading to computational inefficiency.
<span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Crucially, existing agentic frameworks lack a unified mechanism to discipline the exploration process. Consequently, they often suffer from inefficient, random probing trajectories that fail to systematically bridge the gap between abstract logical planning and concrete data-level constraints through a coherent hypothesis-verification loop.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Methodology</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section details how <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> applies agentic exploration to schema linking and SQL generation through a hypothesis-verification loop. Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Pre-processed Schema Augmentation. ‣ 2. Related Work ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the framework of <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>Problem Formulation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> denote a natural language question. The target database is structured as a set of tables <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\{T_{1},\dots,T_{m}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\{T_{1},\dots,T_{m}\}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            To simplify notation, <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> includes both schema and data; real data is accessed only during agentic exploration.</span></span></span>, where each table <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{j}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{j}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math> consists of columns along with their respective metadata (e.g., types and descriptions). <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> addresses two sequential objectives. The first is <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">schema linking</span>, which aims to identify a sufficient column set <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{*}\subset\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>⊂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{*}\subset\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> that maximizes the recall of columns relevant to the question while minimizing the number of columns. The second is <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">SQL generation</span>, which focuses on synthesizing a correct query requested by <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> against <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">H</span><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ypothesis-<span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">V</span>erification (H-V).</span>
Ambiguous naming in enterprise databases often obscures true semantics, necessitating a direct and data-driven interpretation.
To enable effective agentic exploration over large-scale schemas, we introduce a unified <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hypothesis–verification</span> loop, in which the system actively interacts with the database to iteratively refine its understanding.
Importantly, this agentic exploration is explicitly instantiated at two critical stages of the Text-to-SQL pipeline: <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">schema linking</em> and <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">SQL generation</em>.
We detail the design of agentic exploration for schema linking and SQL generation separately in the following subsections.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>Agentic Exploration for Schema Linking</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To navigate large-scale enterprise databases with ambiguous naming conventions and complex structures, <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> instantiates <em id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">agentic exploration within the schema linking stage</em> through the H-V loop.
Specifically, <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> generates schema-agnostic hypotheses in the form of logical plans, which are subsequently grounded and validated against the database.
To further streamline this verification process, <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> introduces a Dual-Pathway Pruning mechanism prior to verification.
The following sections provide a detailed breakdown of each component (Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Pre-processed Schema Augmentation. ‣ 2. Related Work ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (Top)).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1. </span>Hypothesis Generation via Logical Planning</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Directly mapping a query onto a massive schema forces the LLM to conflate retrieval and reasoning, often resulting in suboptimal outcomes. This coupling obscures implicit intermediate steps and exacerbates <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">schema bias</span>, wherein LLMs hallucinate spurious connections based on superficial string-level similarities.
To address this issue, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> introduces a dedicated <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Logical Planning</span> stage.
Specifically, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> first generates a schema-agnostic plan that hypothesizes the required computational steps and latent constraints, deliberately isolating high-level reasoning from the noise introduced by concrete table and column names.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure the derived plan covers all potential logical branches required to answer the query, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> employs a consensus-based synthesis strategy where multiple reasoning paths are aggregated into a unified master plan. Formally, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> generates <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> independent candidates <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{P^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{P^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}</annotation></semantics></math> where each candidate is sampled from <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,F^{sl}_{plan})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,F^{sl}_{plan})</annotation></semantics></math>. These candidates are then integrated into a master plan <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>P</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> through a secondary inference process defined by</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(1)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="P^{*}=p_{\theta}\left(\cdot\mid q,\{P^{(1)},\dots,P^{(N)}\},F^{sl}_{agg}\right),\vskip-2.84526pt" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P^{*}=p_{\theta}\left(\cdot\mid q,\{P^{(1)},\dots,P^{(N)}\},F^{sl}_{agg}\right),\vskip-2.84526pt</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">with <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> the LLM and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{sl}_{\text{plan}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mtext>plan</mtext><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{sl}_{\text{plan}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{sl}_{\text{agg}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mtext>agg</mtext><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{sl}_{\text{agg}}</annotation></semantics></math> instruction templates.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2. </span>Search Space Reduction via Dual-Pathway Pruning</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Exhaustive data exploration is computationally prohibitive, which motivates <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> to introduce a preliminary filtration step. However, standard relevance filtering is prone to false negatives, often discarding foreign keys that lack both lexical and semantic alignment with the query terms. To address this issue, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> employs a <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dual-Pathway Pruning</span> strategy. Specifically, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> simultaneously executes a negative pass to remove obvious noise and a positive pass to identify relevant items, and subsequently fuses the results from both passes.
Let <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{B_{1},\dots,B_{K}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{B_{1},\dots,B_{K}\}</annotation></semantics></math> represent <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> manageable batches partitioned from the schema <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, where each batch consists of a subset of columns. For each batch <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> identifies a deletion set of columns <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{del,j}\subseteq B_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⊆</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{del,j}\subseteq B_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> and a preservation set of columns <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{keep,j}\subseteq B_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⊆</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{keep,j}\subseteq B_{j}</annotation></semantics></math>. The pruned schema <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{pruned}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{pruned}</annotation></semantics></math> is then formulated as:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E2X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="3" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_left">(2)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{del,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{del,j}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,P^{*},B_{j},F^{sl}_{del})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,P^{*},B_{j},F^{sl}_{del})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E2Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{keep,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{keep,j}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,P^{*},B_{j},F^{sl}_{sel})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,P^{*},B_{j},F^{sl}_{sel})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E2Xb" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2Xb.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{pruned}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{pruned}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2Xb.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\bigcup_{j=1}^{K}\left((B_{j}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{del,j})\cup\mathcal{C}_{keep,j}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">⋃</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∖</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\bigcup_{j=1}^{K}\left((B_{j}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{del,j})\cup\mathcal{C}_{keep,j}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where the union logic ensures that any ambiguous element is preserved unless it is both confidently rejected as noise and fails to be explicitly recognized as task-critical.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.3. </span>Hypothesis Verification via Agentic Exploration</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify hypotheses in the logical plan over <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{pruned}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{pruned}</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> employs <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agentic Exploration</span>, starting with <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Semantic Linking</span>. In this step, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> hypothesizes the specific role of each table and column, such as serving as the primary filter.
This role mapping establishes the direction for the subsequent <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parallel Data Profiling</span>, in which <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> assigns independent agents to each table, restricted to the subset of columns in <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{pruned}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{pruned}</annotation></semantics></math>. Unlike static profiling, these agents dynamically generate SQL queries grounded in the hypothesized roles to verify data patterns. Following this local exploration, the <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Global Synthesis</span> phase enables <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> to integrate the entire <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{pruned}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{pruned}</annotation></semantics></math> along with their respective empirical observations, and to make the final decision on the sufficient subgraph <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This process can be formulated as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">

<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the functional role analysis, and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the empirical observations for each candidate table <math id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Agentic Exploration for SQL Generation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To translate abstract user intent into executable SQL under rigid schema constraints, <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> instantiates <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">agentic exploration within the SQL generation stage</em> through the H-V loop.
Specifically, <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> interleaves reasoning and exploration to actively synthesize hypotheses and validate them through evidence-driven query execution (Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Pre-processed Schema Augmentation. ‣ 2. Related Work ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (Bottom)).
To ensure meaningful exploration, <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> first retrieves question-relevant guidance that constrains the search space and prevents superficial or degenerate probing.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.1. </span>Guidance via Deterministic Retrieval</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Exploration is only effective when the agent knows <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">what</span> to verify. Without explicit guidance, models are prone to overlooking critical constraints such as integer division truncation or case-sensitivity. To address this limitation, <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> introduces a <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Deterministic Retrieval</span> mechanism that leverages the logical plan (Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS1" title="3.2.1. Hypothesis Generation via Logical Planning ‣ 3.2. Agentic Exploration for Schema Linking ‣ 3. Methodology ‣ APEX-SQL: Talking to the data via Agentic Exploration for Text-to-SQL" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.1</span></a>) to retrieve query-dependent exploration guidance.
Specifically, <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> infers potential SQL realization paths for each logical step, such as implementing “ranking” using the <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">RANK()</span> function over the <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">score</span> column.
Based on these realizations, <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> applies a rule engine to extract and match operational keywords against a predefined library, such that detecting a <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">RANK</span> keyword activates specific directives, including inspecting <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">NULL</span> values in the corresponding column.
This process is formulated as:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E4X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_left">(4)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{W}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\text{ExtractKeywords}\!\left(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,P^{*},\mathcal{D}^{*},F^{sql}_{kw})\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mpadded style="width:7.968em;" width="7.968em"><mtext>ExtractKeywords</mtext></mpadded><mo>(</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>P</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>F</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msup><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\text{ExtractKeywords}\!\left(p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,P^{*},\mathcal{D}^{*},F^{sql}_{kw})\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E4Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E4Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\{m\in\mathcal{M}\mid\text{Match}(\mathcal{W},m)=\text{True}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>Match</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>True</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\{m\in\mathcal{M}\mid\text{Match}(\mathcal{W},m)=\text{True}\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of operational keywords, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{sql}_{kw}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{sql}_{kw}</annotation></semantics></math> is the instruction template, and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> represents a library of SQL best practices.
Since SQL operations constitute a finite and closed set, <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> adopts deterministic keyword mapping to achieve higher reliability than dense retrieval, which often introduces irrelevant noise.
As a result, <span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">APEX-SQL</span> transforms the logical plan from a passive blueprint into an executable verification guide, ensuring that exploration remains focused on relevant technical risks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
